nav.label: Main navigation
level.very_strong.help: Deliberately excessive: unlocking the key takes a few seconds and a lot of memory, which makes guessing the passphrase extremely slow.
level.strong.help: What we recommend: no known attack, unlocks in under a second.
level.medium.help: Still safe today, with less margin: RSA-2048 is the minimum still accepted, and PBKDF2 is easier to attack with graphics cards than Argon2id.
level.weak.help: For teaching only: without a salt, the same passphrase always gives the same lock, so an attacker can precompute guesses once and reuse them against everyone.
level.none.help: The private key is stored in clear on disk: anyone who copies the key file can read everything sent to you. Never recommended.
level.custom.help: Your own settings: the level shown is that of the weakest setting.
rating.title: Security level:
rating.no_passphrase: No passphrase: anyone who copies the key file can open all your files.
rating.key_type.x25519: X25519: modern elliptic curve, about 128-bit security, small and fast keys.
rating.key_type.rsa-4096: RSA 4096-bit: very strong, but slow to generate.
rating.key_type.rsa-3072: RSA 3072-bit: recommended size for RSA (128-bit security).
rating.key_type.rsa-2048: RSA 2048-bit: the minimum still accepted (112-bit security).
rating.cipher.aes-256-gcm: AES-256-GCM: encrypts the file and detects any modification.
rating.cipher.aes-128-gcm: AES-128-GCM: also safe, with less margin than AES-256.
rating.kdf.argon2id: Argon2id: memory-hard, graphics cards barely help an attacker.
rating.kdf.pbkdf2-sha256: PBKDF2: fine, but easier to attack with graphics cards.
rating.kdf_strength.max: Maximum strength: each attacker guess costs a few seconds.
rating.kdf_strength.strong: High strength: unlocks in about one second.
rating.kdf_strength.normal: Normal strength: unlocks in about half a second.
rating.salt.0: No salt: an attacker can precompute guesses once for everyone.
protect.passphrase_help: At least 12 characters (16 for “Very strong”), no symbols required: an easy-to-remember sentence works very well. It never leaves your PC.
protect.no_passphrase_warning: Warning: the private key will be stored unprotected. Anyone who copies the key file will be able to open every file sent to you.
protect.no_passphrase_confirm: I understand, store it without a passphrase
protect.kdf_help: Turns your passphrase into a lock, deliberately slowly, to slow down an attacker.

info.title: How it works
info.keys_intro: Each user has a key pair:
info.public_key_text: is shared freely: it is used to encrypt files for you;
info.private_key_text: stays on your computer, locked by your passphrase: only it can decrypt.
info.only_public_shared: The only thing you share is your public key: no passphrase ever travels.
info.hybrid_step1: A random key is drawn, a new one for each file.
info.hybrid_step2: The file is encrypted with this key (AES-GCM), in 64 KiB chunks: each chunk is protected against modification.
info.hybrid_step3: This key is locked with the recipient's public key (RSA-OAEP, or X25519 + HKDF): that's key.enc.
info.hybrid_step4: To open it, the recipient's private key recovers the file key, which opens the file.
info.hybrid_why: Why two steps? Public-key encryption is slow and limited in size; AES is fast on large files. We combine both.
info.levels_intro: You can pick a level instead of setting each option. Changing an option by hand switches to “Custom”, and the level shown becomes that of the weakest setting.
info.levels_note: The key type and protection are chosen when creating the key; the file encryption (AES-256 or AES-128) when encrypting.
info.salt_text1: Without a salt, the same passphrase always gives the same lock: an attacker can precompute guesses once (rainbow tables) and reuse them against everyone.
info.salt_text2: With a random salt, each guess only works for one key: everything has to start over for the next one.
info.fingerprint_text1: The fingerprint is a unique summary of the public key (SHA-256), identical on every machine. When you add a contact, compare it with them out loud.
info.fingerprint_text2: If someone swapped the key while it was being sent (email, messaging…), the fingerprints won't match: it's the only way to detect this “man-in-the-middle” attack.
info.format_intro: An ordinary zip, uncompressed, bundling 2 files (3 if signed). Its name doesn't matter: a renamed package decrypts the same.
info.format_key: The file's random key, encrypted with the recipient's public key.
info.format_file: A header (public settings, no secret), then the file encrypted in chunks, with its original name inside.
info.format_sig: (bonus, optional) The sender's signature over both files.
info.format_note: Each chunk is checked together with the header: changing a setting or a single byte makes the package unreadable, and nothing is decrypted.
info.tip1: Back up your private key (My keys → Export private key) on a device you own: if you lose it, or forget its passphrase, the files encrypted for you are lost. Nobody can recover them.
info.tip2: Never send your private key to anyone.
info.tip3: A long passphrase is better than a complicated password.
info.tip4: Check each contact's fingerprint before trusting it.
info.not1: send the files: you send the package yourself (email, USB stick…);
info.not2: protect a computer that is already infected: spyware can read the key while it is unlocked;
info.not3: hide that a file was exchanged, or its approximate size;
info.not4: open files encrypted by other tools (GPG, age, 7-Zip…).
